entries.notes_md:
- **The screen can now turn off on its own hours.** On the Screensaver card,
  "When the screen may turn off" can follow the screensaver's hours (as
  before), allow any time, or use its own hours. So the screensaver can run
  all day while the screen only turns off after hours, and it comes back on
  when those hours end. Displays keep their current behaviour until this is
  changed.
- **Displays are ready to take settings sent from the management console**
  (the page, permissions, screensaver, keyboard, clock and admin password),
  so they can be changed on many displays at once. A display checks every
  value before changing anything, and changes nothing if any value is
  wrong. Sending settings from the console is not switched on yet.

- **Displays can now take actions sent from the management console**, such as
  a hard reload, restarting the browser or restarting the display, so they
  can be applied to many displays at once. A display runs only an action that
  is signed by the management server, meant for that display, recent, and
  allowed for the person who sent it; it never runs the same action twice,
  and it reports back whether each one worked. Sending actions from the
  console is not switched on yet.

- **Displays now report whether they can be woken over the network.** Each
  display tells the management console whether its network card supports
  wake-on-LAN, whether it is switched on, and the address to send the wake to,
  so a display that has gone dark can be woken remotely where the hardware
  allows it.
- **Less is sent to the management console.** The video check result and the
  wake-on-LAN details are sent only when they change, plus once a day,
  instead of with every hourly check-in.
- **The video check is fairer.** It lets the video settle for a second before
  measuring and tries both sizes every time, so a display that plays 1080p
  smoothly is no longer marked down by a slow start. Every display checks once
  more at its next startup.

- **The video check is stricter, and its result now reaches the management
  console.** A display whose video engine can't count the frames it shows,
  or whose picture is frozen or black, no longer counts as playing video. The
  check runs once more at the next startup so every display is measured the
  same way. The result now reaches the management console with the display's
  regular check-in, so it can be seen for the whole fleet. It still only
  measures; nothing about how a page or its videos play has changed.

- **Each display now checks how well it can play video, and reports it.** Once
  at startup, and again after an operating system update or when someone
  presses **Re-check video** on the Display card, a display plays a short
  test clip for about 15 seconds before its page appears, and records whether
  it plays video smoothly at 720p and at 1080p. The Display card shows the
  result. This only measures: nothing about how a page or its videos play
  has changed.

- **A display only installs an operating system update built for its own
  hardware.** This gets things ready for SteadyScreen on more kinds of
  hardware. Every display checks that an OS update matches the machine it is
  running on, both when it downloads the update and again before it installs
  it, and refuses one that does not.
- **An update that states a minimum OS version the display can't read is now
  refused, instead of being treated as having no minimum.** Nothing published
  today is affected; this closes a gap before it could matter.
- **The boot-path migration tool refuses to run on hardware it wasn't made
  for**, rather than trying and leaving the display unable to start.

- **Displays installed since mid-September report their update channel
  again.** The installer left the display's update settings readable only by
  the system, so the display couldn't read them itself. Updates kept working,
  but the display's channel showed blank in the management console and its
  Updates settings showed defaults. The display now puts that right on its
  next update check.

- **Installing is about a minute quicker, and the boot splash step shows
  once.** Turning on the boot splash at the end of an install rebuilt part of
  the system that was already ready, which took close to a minute on slower
  machines. It now skips that when nothing has changed.
- **The boot splash is fixed SteadyScreen branding.** The hidden settings
  that could replace or remove it on a display are gone. The SteadyScreen
  logo on the welcome and admin pages is unchanged.

- **Installing is about a minute quicker, and the boot splash step shows
  once.** Turning on the boot splash at the end of an install rebuilt part of
  the system that the installer already had ready, which took close to a
  minute on slower machines. It now skips that when nothing has changed.

- **ScreenConnect now shows the display's real screen on every machine.** On
  some displays (seen on portrait ones) the ScreenConnect thumbnail was
  missing and joining showed a black landscape screen, because the agent was
  picking the console framebuffer instead of the picture on screen. The
  agent relies on a small system command to find the right screen, and the
  image didn't have it. The display now supplies it. Proven on a store display
  that had it: thumbnail and live view back without switching sessions by hand.

- **The clock screensaver shows the full date with the year**, as
  "Thursday September 24, 2026" (it was "Thursday 24 September").
- **The SSH "Log in as" line no longer points at the wrong machine when the
  admin page is opened through remote admin.** It printed the remote-admin
  address, which leads to the server rather than the display. It now shows the
  display's own network address, and says SSH only works from the display's
  own network.

- **"Turn the screen off after" now puts the TV into standby over HDMI-CEC.**
  On a display with a CEC adapter, the screen-off timer sends the TV to
  standby as well as switching the picture off, instead of leaving a lit
  "no signal" screen. Whatever brings the screen back also wakes the TV: a
  touch, the screensaver hours ending, the setting being switched off, or the
  display restarting. It only wakes a TV that the display itself put into
  standby, so a TV the shop turned off with its own remote is left alone.
  Displays without CEC behave exactly as before. Proven on an office test
  display with a Pulse-Eight adapter: standby, wake, and wake after a restart.

- **Pinch-to-zoom is now actually held on a touch panel.** The lock (off by
  default) stops a customer pinching the page out of shape and leaving it that
  way. WebKit on a touch panel ignored the page-level block, and a pinch scales
  the page rather than the browser zoom, so the earlier browser-zoom clamp missed
  it too. The display now intercepts the two-finger gesture itself, before WebKit
  can assemble it into a zoom. Proven on a real touch panel: with the lock on a
  pinch does nothing and a one-finger scroll still works; with the lock off pinch
  zooms normally.

- **You can clear a display's page now, and it drops back to the welcome
  screen.** Leaving the page URL blank in the admin used to be rejected, so once
  a page was set the only move was to point it somewhere else. Now a blank URL
  clears it and the display shows its welcome screen again -- and the admin shows
  a cleared page as an empty box and "Welcome screen", not the literal
  "about:blank" or an internal address.

- **Pinch-to-zoom is held at the browser level, not just the page.** The lock
  (off by default) put a no-zoom viewport on the customer's page, but on a touch
  panel WebKit ignored it and a customer could still pinch the page out of shape.
  The display now also snaps the zoom back whenever the lock is on, so a pinch no
  longer sticks.

- **The "checking for updates" screen no longer has a red border.** That red edge
  means "the page is unreachable"; it belongs on a customer's page, not on one of
  our own setup screens, which already say in words what the network is doing. It
  was suppressed on the welcome and startup screens but had been missed on this
  one.

- **A standalone display no longer shows the "belongs to an existing account"
  notice.** A layout bug left that notice on screen on every display from the
  moment it loaded -- including displays that are in nobody's account. Now it
  appears only when a display genuinely was reinstalled while claimed to an
  account, and then it takes the place of the "link to an account" box rather
  than sitting beside it. The wording is shorter, and it shows the display's
  device key so you can check it against the one your account shows.

- **The device key and the account pairing code are now clearly different
  things.** The 12-character value derived from a display's key is called the
  "device key" everywhere -- the setup screen, the admin page (it had been
  mislabeled "pairing code"), and the reinstalled notice -- and the account
  pairing code stays the account pairing code. One is how you confirm a display's
  identity; the other is how you link a new display to an account.

- **A ScreenConnect agent that installs but dies is now brought back
  automatically.** ConnectWise's own postinstall sometimes leaves the service
  dead a few seconds after a fresh convert first comes up -- which is why a new
  display so often had to have "Restart service" pressed by hand before it
  appeared in the console. Every display now checks on each update pass whether
  its agent is installed-but-stopped and restarts it, retrying until it stays up.
  Because it rides the ordinary software update, a display already in the field
  self-heals at its next check -- no reflash -- and it keeps watch afterwards, so
  an agent that dies later comes back on its own. (Delivered as a component; a
  display gets it on whichever channel it tracks.)

- **First-boot enrolment retries until the agent is actually running**, instead
  of trusting a single delayed restart. On a machine installed from a new image,
  the agent comes up within a minute or two of first boot and is confirmed to
  stay up before the enrolment step stands down.

- **The installer now asks which updates a display should receive.** Stable
  (strongly recommended) or Testing (risky). Stable stays the default and is what
  a store display should be on; Testing is the opt-in for a bench display that
  needs unreleased software. The from-Windows converter shows the same choice,
  and a batch file that says nothing still installs Stable exactly as before.

This release ships with a new OS image (os 1.4.6). The software is delivered as
normal signed components; the image is what carries the parts a component cannot
install for itself — the first-boot gate and the ScreenConnect first-boot
enrolment — so a machine gets the full behaviour only when it is installed from
this image.

- **A fresh display checks for updates before it shows the setup screen.** On the
  very first boot it briefly says "checking for updates" and applies anything
  waiting, so a new install lands current instead of coming up on the image's
  baked-in software and only catching up hours later at its first update window.
  It never strands the boot: no network, or nothing to fetch, and it goes
  straight on to setup.

- **The installer no longer asks for a Display name.** The setup screens now show
  the machine's own hostname (ds-hwid) instead. A name typed at install time was
  only ever a second label for the same box; the admin page can still set a
  friendly name whenever you want one.

- **A reinstalled display that belongs to an account waits for the owner to
  approve it.** Reinstalling or resetting a claimed display mints a new device
  key; rather than trusting whoever reflashed it, the server holds the new key
  pending and the account owner approves the change from their own portal — no
  call to us. A standalone display (in nobody's account) still just pairs, so a
  forgotten admin password is always recoverable by reinstalling.

- **Wake-on-LAN is enabled on supported wired machines (x86).** A display on
  hardware we control can be woken from the LAN after it is powered off. It
  detects and reports whether the machine is even a candidate — firmware still
  has to keep the NIC powered in S5 — so you can tell which displays WoL can
  actually reach rather than finding out a BIOS setting did nothing.

- **Restarting the browser now waits until the page is back before it reports
  done**, the same way reboot and update already do, instead of returning while
  the screen is still black.

- **A freshly enrolled display restarts its ScreenConnect agent once, by
  itself.** ConnectWise's installer can leave the service dead a few seconds
  after first boot, which is why a new convert so often needed the admin page's
  "Restart service" pressed by hand before it appeared in the console. The
  display now does that press automatically, once, after the agent has settled.

- **The page-reload settings moved to the Page tab and got clearer.** Two
  separate things now, instead of one vague "auto-reload":
  - **Idle reset** returns the display to its page after it has been idle for a
    while -- a kiosk going back to its login screen. A normal reload.
  - **Auto-reload** does a hard refresh to pick up a new version of the web app,
    on whichever trigger you choose: after the display has been idle, or at a set
    time of day. By default it only reloads while the page is reachable, so it
    never refreshes onto a blank screen.

- **Pinch-to-zoom can be turned off, and is off by default.** Under Permissions:
  a customer at a touch display can no longer pinch the page out of shape and
  leave it that way for the next person. Turn it back on for a display where
  pinching is wanted.

- **Screen rotation now holds across a reboot, and Portrait means Portrait.**
  Two fixes for the rotation setting, both found on a converted display:
  - **It sticks now, even without a touchscreen.** On a marketing or menu board
    (no touchscreen at all), setting a rotation turned the screen but did not
    survive the next reboot -- it came back Landscape -- because a "no
    touchscreen" result was mistaken for a failure and the setting was never
    saved. Whether the screen actually turned is now what counts, so the
    rotation is written down and re-applied on every boot.
  - **Portrait and Portrait (flipped) were the wrong way round.** A panel that
    Windows called "Portrait" only came up right-side-up if you chose "Portrait
    (flipped)". They are corrected, so the label matches the physical result --
    choose Portrait for a Windows-Portrait panel.

- The **Screen rotation** setting now uses the same words as Windows --
  **Landscape**, **Portrait**, **Landscape (flipped)**, **Portrait (flipped)**
  -- instead of "90 left / 90 right". It matches what the same panel was set to
  under Windows, so there is nothing to translate. Nothing about how a display
  rotates changed; only the labels.

- **Machines converted from Windows now come up on whatever Wi-Fi they were on,
  open networks included.** The installer keeps the exact connection it used to
  reach the network rather than assuming a WPA2 password -- so an open network,
  or a WPA3 one, is no longer left unable to rejoin the network it was installed
  over. (This is in the installer, so it applies to new conversions, not to a
  display that is already running.)

- The **Rollback snapshots** card lists the saved snapshots again. A display
  that had taken three or more of them -- by now, every display -- showed
  "None yet" even though the snapshots were there and an undo would have
  worked: the page was cutting the list off before it could be read. The
  snapshots themselves were never touched, and a rollback still worked from
  the command line the whole time; this only restores the page's view of them.

- The Remote support card now has two buttons to recover the ScreenConnect
  agent without a reboot: **Restart service** and **Reinstall agent**. On a
  fresh install the agent can install but not come up (ConnectWise's service
  does not retry itself), and until now the only fix was a reboot -- which the
  displays this ships to have nobody to do. Now it is a button on the admin
  page, the one channel that stays reachable when ScreenConnect does not. The
  buttons appear once an agent is installed.

- A newly set-up display now checks for the latest software as soon as it comes
  online and updates itself right away, instead of waiting for its next hourly
  check.
- A newly set-up display now sends its first heartbeat the moment it comes
  online, instead of waiting up to five minutes, so it appears in your fleet
  right away.
- The ScreenConnect agent a new display installs is now reliably started, is
  retried every minute until it enrols (so the tile appears in a minute or two,
  not ten), and can now show the display's screen in your console instead of a
  black frame.

- A newly set-up display now checks for the latest software as soon as it comes
  online and updates itself right away, instead of waiting for its next hourly
  check.
- The ScreenConnect agent a new display installs is now reliably started and can
  show the display's screen in your console.

- Turning the SSH server on from the Remote access card now shows correctly as
  running. On the previous version it could briefly read "inactive" just after
  you turned it on, though SSH was in fact up.

- The SSH server on/off switch in the Remote access card now works on displays
  that were updated in place, not only freshly imaged ones. Where it cannot act,
  it greys out and says why instead of looking like it works.

- A newly set-up or converted display now connects to your ScreenConnect
  console by itself on first boot, so you have a way to reach it even before it
  has checked in — and a display converted from Windows comes back as the same
  console entry it was, not a new one. (Turned on per install by your own
  setup; a plain display with no console configured does nothing here.)
- Displays on AMD graphics hardware now load the proper graphics driver.
  Nothing on screen changes on the machines that already worked; this prevents
  a blank screen on some AMD models.
- Staff can turn the display's own SSH server on or off from the Remote access
  card. The admin page and ScreenConnect keep working either way.
- A test print to a printer that is not ready now reports "not ready" plainly
  instead of looking like a server error.
- After an update, a display reports its new version to your management account
  straight away, instead of up to five minutes later.

- The Account pairing card is tidied: the staff device-key and remote-session
  details are removed from it, and the "linked to your account" line now shows
  "Checking account link…" until your management server reports the link, so a
  linked display never briefly reads "Not linked" by mistake.

- The System tab now opens on the Status card, and the old "Remote admin"
  section is folded into "Account pairing" — which now shows which SteadyScreen
  account and location this display is linked to, once it is linked.
- Any change made on the display now updates your management account straight
  away, instead of waiting for its next hourly check-in. Nothing on the display's
  own screen changes.

- Your team can now open a display's admin page from your SteadyScreen account,
  and what each person can change depends on their role. Owners and operators
  get everything except the SSH settings; a user can see the page and its
  status and run printer test prints, and can change the displayed page only if
  you give them that permission. Nothing on the display's own screen changes.

- A display with no page set now shows a pairing code on its own screen. Enter
  that code at ssm.steadyscreen.com/activate to link the display to your
  SteadyScreen account.
- The admin page has a new "Account pairing" card with a "Show pairing code"
  button, to link a display that already has a page — and to move a display
  that is linked to another account, by asking that owner to release it.

- When you change something on a display — its page, or any setting — it now
  tells your management account straight away, instead of at its next hourly
  check-in. Nothing on the screen changes.

- The display now tells your management account which page it is set to show,
  so that address appears on the display's card in your account. Nothing on
  the screen changes, and a display that has no page set yet reports nothing.

- Remote admin: after the owner approves a display on the fleet page, the
  display now notices within a few minutes instead of up to an hour. It
  checks in more often only while it is waiting to be approved, and only for
  its first day up. Nothing else changes.

- 1.15.0 is the first release in which displays genuinely work with the
  management server, gathered under one milestone version. It carries the
  remote-admin work that was on testing as 1.14.137-1.14.144: each display's
  own device key (approved once from the fleet page by a 12-character pairing
  code), the doorbell, the relay client that shows the display's real admin
  page through the server, and the touch-calibration safeguards. The code is
  byte-for-byte what ran on testing as 1.14.144; only the version changes.
  Nothing appears on a display's own screen, and nothing opens until the
  display is approved.

- Remote admin: the touch-screen calibration button is now hidden when the
  admin page is viewed remotely, since calibration must be measured at the
  display. It was already refused server-side; now it is not offered either.
  Nothing else changes.

- Remote admin safety: the touch-screen calibration tool can no longer be
  used through a remote admin session. A calibration has to be measured by
  touching the display itself; one measured in a remote browser would leave
  the store's screen mis-aligned. Nothing else changes.

- Remote admin: the display now reads the server's "you may connect" message
  correctly (its expiry is a date, which an earlier build misread), and it
  refuses one whose expiry is implausibly far ahead, so a stray or replayed
  message can never open a display. Nothing appears on the display's screen.

- Remote admin, step 3: an approved display can now, when the owner opens it
  from the fleet page, connect out to the management server and show its real
  admin page there. It replays each request inside its own process, with no
  network port opened on the display. Nothing appears on the display's own
  screen. It does nothing until a session is opened, and only for an approved
  display with remote admin left on.

- Remote admin: when the management server restarts, an approved display
  now reconnects within seconds instead of waiting five minutes.
- The admin page, when shown remotely through the management server, no
  longer tries to jump to another port after an update.

- Each display now shows a 12-character pairing code, for approving it once
  on the fleet page: large at the top of the admin page's System tab, and on
  the setup screens. The fleet page shows the same code, so approving is a
  matter of checking the two match.
- A display that has been approved now remembers it across a restart,
  instead of waiting up to an hour to hear it again from the server.

- Remote admin, step 2. Once the owner has approved a display on the fleet
  page, the display keeps one quiet request open to the management server,
  so the server can reach it within seconds when remote admin is used.
  Nothing appears on screen. It does nothing until the display is approved,
  and nothing more until remote admin itself, the next step, is released.

- Each display now makes its own device key the first time it starts on
  this version, and shows its fingerprint on the admin page (System tab,
  Remote admin). The public half goes with the heartbeat, so the owner can
  approve each display once on the fleet page. The private key never leaves
  the display. Remote admin itself is not here yet.

- The display's heartbeat to the management server now also carries the
  display's address on its own local network (for example 192.0.2.50),
  so the fleet page can link to its admin page. Only a private local
  address is ever sent -- never a public internet address. Nothing else is
  added.

- The display's heartbeat to the management server now also carries the
  display's own name (the ds- name it shows on screen) and whether it takes stable or
  testing updates. Nothing else is added. Either is left out when the
  display cannot read it truthfully.

- The display's heartbeat to the management server now also carries the
  date the display was installed and how long it has been running since it
  last started. Nothing else is added. Either is left out when the display
  cannot read it truthfully.

- The display's status API no longer reports its heartbeat to the management
  server: not the message it last sent, not when, and not the result. The
  heartbeat itself is unchanged and still sends only the display's id, its
  software version and its OS version.

- Displays can now receive and keep a signed activation date from the
  SteadyScreen management server, and let other displays on the same network
  read it. It is the groundwork for the free-display limit per location.
  Nothing on the screen changes, and no display limits itself in this release.

- The Management server card is gone from the System tab. On the testing
  channel every display reports to the SteadyScreen management server, as the
  owner decided, and there is no switch to turn it off. What it sends is still
  only the display's id, its software version and its OS version.

- Displays now report to the SteadyScreen management server at
  ssm.steadyscreen.com by default: once a day, just the display's id, its
  software version and its OS version. The Management server card on the
  System tab shows exactly what was sent. Clearing the address, or switching
  the heartbeat off, stops it.

- The display can now tell a SteadyScreen management server that it exists.
  Once a day it sends its id, its software version and its OS version —
  nothing else — and the System tab has a new **Management server** card that
  shows exactly what was sent and when, with a switch to turn it off.
- Nothing is sent until a server address is set, and none is set by default.
  Whatever the server does, the display's own page is never affected.

- Text on the admin page no longer breaks in the middle of words. Longer
  messages, such as the Display tab's note about the TV's HDMI-CEC setting,
  now wrap between words like normal text. Long addresses and keys still wrap
  so they fit on a phone.

- A Pulse-Eight USB HDMI-CEC adapter now works. Plug it in between the display
  and the TV and the display finds it and sets it up by itself, so the Wake and
  Standby buttons on the Display tab turn the TV on and off.
- The Display tab now tells you whether the TV itself is listening. If the
  TV's own HDMI-CEC setting is switched off, it says so and names the setting
  to turn on — SIMPLINK on LG, Anynet+ on Samsung, BRAVIA Sync on Sony —
  instead of the buttons silently doing nothing.

- Holding a finger on the saved page to reach the setup screen no longer keeps
  it there. The display waits another minute and, if the site still cannot be
  reached, goes back to showing the menu. A customer who holds the glass on an
  offline kiosk can no longer leave a display stuck on a diagnostics screen.
- Anyone actually working on the machine is not interrupted: every touch puts
  the minute back to the start. To stop it altogether, press **Scan for
  networks** and then **Stay on this screen**.
- That stop now lasts for the outage rather than until the display is
  restarted. As soon as the site can be reached again, everything holding the
  saved page back is released.

- The saved page now comes up when a display loses its site **while it is
  running**, not only when it reboots with the network already down. A menu
  board that has been up for a week and loses its connection waits a minute
  and then shows the last picture of the menu, framed in red, instead of
  sitting on the network diagnostic screen.
- The minute is counted from when the diagnostic screen appeared, so a brief
  connection hiccup cannot put a photograph up in place of a live page, and
  touching the screen still starts the minute again.

- The on-screen keyboard now puts itself away after 30 seconds with nothing
  typed, so it stops covering half the page when nobody is using it. Typing,
  or touching the screen, keeps it up.
- If somebody types on a real keyboard plugged into the display, the
  on-screen keyboard gets out of the way. Touching the screen brings it back,
  so a barcode scanner cannot leave a customer without a keyboard.

- The display now answers the usual refresh keys, so a page that has gone
  stale can be reloaded from the display itself without a mouse or a menu.
  F5 or Ctrl+R reloads the page. Ctrl+F5, Shift+F5 or Ctrl+Shift+R reloads it
  ignoring anything saved from last time.
- If the display is showing "cannot reach the site", pressing F5 tries the
  site again rather than reloading that message.

- Fixes the remote-support pop-up that could sit on top of the customer page
  until somebody restarted the display. The display already closes those
  pop-ups by itself; it was closing the first one and then stopping, so every
  one after that stayed on screen.
- After an update, the display now checks that the pop-up closer is actually
  running instead of reporting that it started it. It said it had started on a
  display where it had already stopped.
- Setting up remote support on a display now checks the pop-up closer is
  installed, and says what to run if it is not. Remote support is what causes
  the pop-ups, so it is where the check belongs.

- Fixes updates never installing on a display that has an admin password set.
  The display installed the update, decided the client had not come back —
  because it asked without signing in and was told 401 — and rolled it back.
  Every night, silently, with nothing to show for it but the old version.
- Two displays were stuck this way. They pick this up on their own at the next
  window and are then able to update normally again.

- Fixes the boot splash being changeable by anything that can reach the
  display. Branding is meant to be managed centrally, and reading it was
  refused — but replacing or deleting it was not. Anything on the same network
  could have cleared a shop's splash.
- Fixes "Wake the display" waking the screen for a second and then letting the
  screensaver straight back. It now stays awake for the same idle time a touch
  on the display would give it. The same fault meant a receipt printing
  brought the page back for only a few seconds.
- The screenshot checkbox is labelled "auto refresh" rather than "live".

- Fixes the boot splash being changeable by anything on the network. Branding
  is meant to be managed centrally, and reading it was refused — but changing
  or removing it was not. Anything that could reach the display could clear a
  shop's splash.
- Adds a screensaver that shows your own picture. It is part of a licensed
  display: on a display without that licence the option is not offered and the
  upload is refused.

- Fixes "Wake the display" waking the screen for a second and then letting the
  screensaver straight back. It now stays awake for the same idle time as a
  touch on the display would give it.
- The same fault meant a receipt printing brought the page back for only a few
  seconds. It now stays up.
- The screenshot checkbox is labelled "auto refresh" rather than "live".

- Fixes the on-screen keyboard being too wide on the admin page, where on a
  1280-wide screen the right-hand keys ran off the edge. It was picking up the
  admin page's own button sizing.

  the admin page, but any page could have done the same.

This is everything since the last stable release, 1.14.105. Nothing here
changes on its own: the screensaver and the power saving are off until you
switch them on.

A screensaver, off unless you turn it on

- There is a Screensaver card on the Display page. Set "Start after" and the
  display shows a screensaver once it has been left alone for that long.
  Touching the screen brings the page straight back, and that first touch is
  not passed on to the page — so waking a display cannot press a button on it.
- Two to choose from: the SteadyScreen mark, and a clock showing the time and
  the date. Both drift slowly around the screen, which also keeps a still page
  from marking the panel. The clock follows the display's own time zone, so if
  it shows the wrong time, check the Clock card.
- It is deliberately not a blank screen. A dark display looks like a broken
  one from across a room.
- You can say when it is allowed to run. Leave it on "any time of day", or set
  hours — a shop that does not want it during trading sets it to run from
  closing until opening, and a window that crosses midnight is fine. If the
  hours end while the screensaver is showing, the display comes back on its
  own rather than waiting for somebody to touch it.
- It never covers the screens the display uses to tell you something — no
  network, the saved page, first-time setup — nor the admin page while
  somebody is on it. If a receipt prints, the screen comes back so you can see
  which display printed it.

Turning the screen off to save power

- The same card can turn the screen off as well. Set "Turn the screen off
  after" and the display goes dark once it has been left alone that long.
  Touching it brings it straight back.
- The two times are independent, both counted from the last touch. Set the
  screen to turn off sooner than the screensaver and the screensaver never
  appears; set it later and the screensaver plays until then. Both keep to the
  hours you set.
- A television shows "no signal" while the screen is off. That is normal, and
  it comes back the moment somebody touches the display — but try it on one
  display before setting it everywhere, because how quickly a screen lights up
  again is down to the screen.
- If the screen has been turned off, the admin page says so, in the live view
  and on the Screensaver card. A display saving power cannot be mistaken there
  for one that has stopped working, because the picture itself cannot show the
  difference.

Installing an update shows what it is doing

- The confirmation box now stays open, reports each step as it happens, says
  when the display is restarting, and reloads the page by itself once the
  display is back. It used to close as soon as you pressed Install and leave
  you with one line while the display went away.
- If the display comes back on the same version it says so, rather than
  reporting success — the update did not take, or something put it back.

Fixes

- Ctrl+Alt+A went to the wrong place when the display was showing one of its
  own screens. On a display sitting on the network screen because its site is
  unreachable, the first press went to that unreachable site and only a second
  press reached the admin page. One press now.
- The admin page can wake a display. When the screensaver is showing, or the
  screen is off, a "Wake the display" button appears beside the screenshot.
- Card headings on the admin page sit on a band of their own, so sections are
  easier to pick out when scrolling.

- Installing an update now shows what it is doing. The confirmation box stays
  open, reports each step as it happens, says when the display is restarting,
  and reloads the page by itself once the display is back.
- If the display comes back on the same version, it says so rather than
  reporting success — the update did not take, or something put it back.

- Installing an update now shows what it is doing. The confirmation box stays
  open and reports each step through to completion, including while the
  display restarts, and the page reloads itself once the display is back.

- Fixes Ctrl+Alt+A going to the wrong place when the display was showing one
  of its own screens. On a display sitting on the network screen because its
  site is unreachable, the first press went to that unreachable site and only
  a second press reached the admin page. One press now.
- The admin page can wake a display. When the screensaver is showing, or the
  screen has been turned off to save power, a "Wake the display" button
  appears beside the screenshot.
- The live view now says when the screen has been turned off to save power.
  The picture cannot show it — turning the screen off does not change what the
  display is drawing — so a display saving power used to look completely
  normal there.

- Card headings on the admin page now sit on a band of their own, so each
  section is easier to pick out when scrolling.

- The SteadyScreen mark is now always the first choice in the Screensaver
  list, whatever else is added to it.

- The screensaver no longer drifts along the same diagonal and back. It sets
  off in a different direction each time, and changes course slightly whenever
  it reaches an edge, so it wanders the whole screen instead of retracing one
  line.
- The clock is a little smaller, which gives it room to move and keeps it
  clear of the edges.
- The Screensaver settings are less wordy.

- A second screensaver: a clock. Pick it under Screensaver on the Display
  page. It shows the time and the date, drifting slowly across the screen the
  same way the SteadyScreen mark does, and it keeps to the same hours.
- The time follows the display's own clock and time zone, so a display set to
  the wrong zone will show the wrong time here too — worth a look at the Clock
  card if it does.

- Fixes the screen never turning off when the screensaver was set to 0. Power
  saving on its own, with no screensaver, did nothing at all — both settings
  read back exactly as you set them, and nothing happened.

- Power saving: the Screensaver card can now turn the screen off as well. Set
  "Turn the screen off after" and the display goes dark once it has been left
  alone that long. Touching it brings the screen straight back.
- The two timers are independent, both counted from the last touch. Set the
  screen to turn off sooner than the screensaver and the screensaver simply
  never appears; set it later and the screensaver plays until then. Both keep
  to the hours you set.
- A television shows "no signal" while the screen is off. That is normal, and
  it comes back the moment somebody touches the display — but try it on one
  display before setting it everywhere, because how quickly a screen lights up
  again is down to the screen.
- If the screen has been turned off to save power, the admin page says so, so
  a display saving power cannot be mistaken for one that has stopped working.
- The Screensaver card now asks which screensaver first and when it should
  start second.

- A screensaver, off unless you turn it on. There is a Screensaver card on the
  Display page: set "Start after" and the SteadyScreen mark drifts slowly
  across the screen once the display has been left alone for that long.
  Touching the screen brings the page straight back, and that first touch is
  not passed on to the page — so waking a display cannot press a button on it.
- You can also say when it is allowed to run. Leave it on "any time of day",
  or set hours — a shop that does not want it during trading sets it to run
  from closing until opening, and a window that crosses midnight is fine. If
  the hours end while the screensaver is showing, the display comes back on
  its own rather than waiting for somebody to touch it.
- It is deliberately not a blank screen. A dark display looks like a broken
  one, and a mark moving across the screen also keeps a still page from
  marking the panel.
- The screensaver never covers the pages the display uses to tell you
  something — no network, the saved page, first-time setup — nor the admin
  page while somebody is on it. If a receipt prints, the screen comes back so
  you can see which display printed it.
- If the display is also set to return to its home page when idle, it now does
  that behind the screensaver, so the page is ready the moment somebody
  touches it.

- The Boot splash card is no longer shown on the admin page. Setting your own
  splash is part of a paid licence and is managed centrally, so there was
  nothing on that card a display could actually do.
- Fixes an update started from the admin page not recording that it happened.
  The display updated correctly, but went on reporting the version it had
  before, and "last checked / last updated" stayed wrong until the next time.
- The updater now keeps a log of what it did, so an update that goes wrong can
  be looked at afterwards instead of guessed at.
- Fixes a display that could go a whole day after an operating-system update
  without its network watchdog, its print-queue recovery, or the settings that
  let it find printers on the network. Those repairs used to run only between
  3am and 5am; they now run whenever the display checks for updates.
- Fixes the Undo button offering to undo an update back to the version the
  display is already running.
- After undoing an update, that version is held back so it is not reinstalled
  overnight. The page now says so, and offers "Install anyway" to take it
  again — you no longer need a command line to get past it. A display never
  reports holding the version it is actually running.
- Only one copy of the ScreenConnect dialog watcher can run at a time.
- Rollback snapshots. The display now keeps what it was before each of its
  last five updates — the software, the system files an update changes, and
  the settings — and any of them can be restored from the admin page. Save
  current state adds one for right now. They cost almost nothing, because
  files that did not change between updates are shared rather than copied.
- The separate settings-only snapshots have been removed from the page. There
  was no way to tell at a glance which of the two would put the software back,
  and only one of them ever did.
- Installing an update now asks first, shows what changed, and says whether it
  can be undone.
- Restarting a display asks first, counts down, and reloads the page by itself
  once the display is back.
- Clearing a stuck USB printer no longer resets the other printer beside it.
- A printer that is busy printing is no longer mistaken for one that has been
  unplugged, which could send a second copy of a receipt to the backup.
- The ScreenConnect "not supported" messages no longer sit on the screen
  waiting for somebody to click OK.
